requirements.text: Proposals must focus on two-year Institutions of Higher Education (IHEs).
Projects must involve partnerships between academic institutions, industry, and economic development agencies.
Courses and programs developed under the grant must be credit-bearing.
Institutions of Higher Education must be accredited in and have a campus located in the US.

Two-year IHEs and their faculty must have significant leadership roles on all projects; if a four-year IHE or non-two-year organization is the fiscal lead, or a secondary institution/school district develops the proposal, two-year IHE (community college) faculty must be identified as Co-PIs.
The ATE program does not support projects focusing on students who will become health, veterinary, or medical technicians.
Programs for the development of baccalaureate degree programs or those focusing solely on pathways to baccalaureate degrees are not eligible.
RAPID, EAGER, and ABR proposals are not appropriate for the ATE program and should not be submitted.
Track 2 (Projects) budget requests must not exceed $1,000,000 over up to three years, and the budget request should match the scope of the project.
Voluntary committed cost sharing is prohibited.
All budget requests must be aligned with the scope of the project.

Funds for equipment and instrumentation normally may not exceed $300,000 for the duration of a full project grant, with exceptions for single pieces costing more than $300,000 if justified for student use/learning outcomes.
Proposers must request educational discounts from equipment suppliers and explain any discount in the budget justification.
Equipment requests must be clearly disclosed in the proposal budget and justified in the budget justification.

NSF project funds may not be used for routine or common items not specific to the project: ordinary teaching activities, general-purpose lab/classroom equipment and software, replacement equipment that doesn't significantly improve instructional capability, vehicles, furnishings, routine supplies, maintenance/service contracts, or construction/renovation of facilities.
Salaries of administrative and clerical staff should normally be treated as indirect costs; direct charging is only appropriate if specific conditions in PAPPG and 2 CFR § 200.413 are met.
Reasonable travel costs, subsistence (lodging and meals), and specific justified stipends per meeting day for participants may be included in project budgets for professional development conferences.
Funds to support an independent evaluator must be requested, matching the scope of proposed evaluative activities developed in partnership with the project team.
An evaluator employed by the home institution is allowed only if they work in a separate organizational unit with a different reporting line.

Proposals must be submitted in accordance with the NSF Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) effective for the relevant due date; meeting PAPPG requirements is the proposer's responsibility.
The Project Description is limited to 15 pages.
A References Cited section must be included, with literature relating specifically to the proposed project's motivation or design; if no references are cited, the section must explicitly state that.

New materials created with grant support must be licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution license (CC BY, CC BY-SA, or CC BY-NC-SA); computer software source code must instead use an open license acceptable to the Free Software Foundation and/or Open Source Initiative.
The Project Summary overview must state the disciplinary focus, activities, and primary audience.
The Project Description must start with the 'Results from Prior NSF Support' subsection, which must include outcomes and metrics for prior NSF awards and other directly impacting awards.

The Project Description must explain the project's motivating rationale, goals, objectives, deliverables, and activities; a timetable and management plan; roles and responsibilities of PI/co-PIs/senior personnel; a sustainability plan; an Evaluation Plan; and a dissemination plan.
The evaluation plan must be included in the Project Description; submitting it as supplementary documentation is not allowed.
The Project Description must include a subsection titled 'Evaluation Plan' detailing specific evaluation requirements.

The Evaluation Plan must address formative and summative evaluation, show clear alignment with project goals/objectives/outcomes/activities, identify specific data sources and instruments, and include a timeline for data collection, reporting, and communication.

Proposals must address issues in one or more of the specified areas: rural technician education, broadening participation (including veterans), recruiting/retaining students with disabilities, or emerging industry needs.
The project must demonstrate institutional impact and potential to impact technician education regionally and/or nationally, including a measurable impact on the local workforce.
Courses developed or updated under the grant must be credit-bearing, with the potential to contribute to or result in an academic credential.

Proposals must demonstrate awareness of prior relevant ATE-funded work and contemporary developments in the field, and should build upon proven educational materials, strategies, and methods where possible.

The Project Description must address what the proposers want to do, why, how, how success will be measured, and the potential benefits, with a well-reasoned, well-organized plan based on sound rationale.
Program Development and Improvement proposals must produce a coherent sequence of classes, laboratories, and work-based educational experiences.
Projects of this type are expected to gather and report on data regarding student completion and initial job placement.
Proposals are expected to communicate a realistic vision and an achievable plan for sustainability.
Proposals should be of the highest quality with the potential to advance or transform frontiers of knowledge.
Projects must contribute more broadly to achieving societal goals through research, directly related activities, or complementary supported activities, with all methods well justified.
Proposals must demonstrate that the individual, team, or organization is well qualified to conduct the proposed activities.
Proposals must demonstrate that adequate resources are available to carry out the proposed activities.
Evidence of institutional and industry support must be clear and compelling, and plans for long-term institutionalization must be addressed.
An assessment of workforce needs for technicians must be conducted, and the project should work with employers to address their current and future needs.
Project results must be widely disseminated, products distributed effectively, and commercialized when appropriate.
The project must promote the participation of the full spectrum of diverse talent in the technical workforce.
Employers in Program Development and Improvement proposals must be committed partners with defined roles, detailed in letters of commitment.
Proposals acquiring instrumentation must include a letter from industry partner(s) describing how workplace needs require the new instrumentation and their role in curricular revisions.
Named evaluators or evaluation teams must have their Biographical Sketches uploaded in 'Other Personnel Biographical Information' in Research.gov using NSF format.
Letters of Collaboration describing expected contributions, roles, and responsibilities are required; nonspecific letters are prohibited.
Proposers must prepare a Data Management and Sharing Plan, which reviewers will evaluate as appropriate.

Submit annual project reports no later than 90 days before each budget period ends, a final project report no later than 120 days after the award expires, and a public project outcomes report no later than 120 days after the award expires, all via Research.gov.
Respond annually to the ATE Annual Survey conducted by the EvaluATE Resource Hub, providing specific data on students, educators, retention, placement, impact, and quality indicators.
Work with ATE Central to archive digital deliverables (e.g., curriculum, materials) by providing copies in an archivable format with clear intellectual property information.
The full proposal must be submitted by the deadline: first Thursday in October, annually (2026-10-01 for this cycle).

## Executive Summary

This document serves as the Final Outcomes Report for the National Science Foundation Advanced Technological Education (NSF ATE) award HCCC-FICT-ATE-2021, titled *Mechatronics Pathways for Rural Manufacturers*. The project period spanned from September 1, 2021, to August 31, 2025. Harrow Creek Community College (HCCC), a public two-year institution serving four rural counties in the Mid-South, executed this initiative under the leadership of Principal Investigator Dr. Renee Okafor, Dean of Workforce and Technical Programs, with Co-Principal Investigator Marcus Lindqvist, Chair of Mechatronics and Industrial Automation.

The primary objective of the award was to develop and implement a sustainable pathway for students entering the mechatronics workforce, specifically targeting employers in rural manufacturing sectors. While the project successfully established foundational curricula, engaged significant industry partners, and achieved notable completion numbers, it did not meet its initial target for student completers. This report provides an honest accounting of these outcomes, detailing the quantitative results, contextual factors influencing enrollment, and the structural assets created during the five-year period.

## Project Goals and Institutional Context

HCCC operates with a mission deeply rooted in serving its regional community, where 52% of the student body receives Pell Grants and 41% are first-generation college students. As of Fall 2025, the institution maintains a credit headcount of 6,840. The *Mechatronics Pathways for Rural Manufacturers* project was designed to address the specific skills gap in local manufacturing by aligning technical education with the needs of rural employers.

The project budget totaled $598,112, funded entirely through the NSF ATE program. Oversight of the financial and administrative aspects was managed by Dana Whitfield, Director of Grants and Sponsored Programs, ensuring compliance with federal regulations and institutional policies. The evaluation of the project’s impact was conducted by Dr. Priya Raman of Bluestem Evaluation Group, providing an independent assessment of the program’s efficacy and reach.

## Quantitative Outcomes: Completions and Placement

The most critical metric for this award was the number of students completing the mechatronics certificate or degree pathway. The original proposal set a target of 120 completers over the five-year period. The final data indicates that 84 students successfully completed the program. While the shortfall is notable, it is essential to contextualize this figure within the broader landscape of workforce development and the specific challenges faced during the project timeline. This indicates that a significant majority of those who finished the program secured employment in fields related to their training, validating the quality and relevance of the curriculum despite the lower volume of graduates. An honest assessment of the project’s performance requires an examination of the factors that contributed to the gap between the 120-completer target and the actual 84 completers. The evaluation conducted by Dr. Priya Raman identified two primary drivers for this variance: macro-environmental enrollment declines and specific operational disruptions within the college. The first two years of the project (2021-2023) coincided with the tail end of the global pandemic and its immediate aftermath. During this period, HCCC experienced a broader institutional trend of enrollment declines across technical and workforce programs. Potential students faced economic instability, health concerns, and shifting priorities that reduced their willingness or ability to enroll in rigorous technical training. This external factor significantly dampened the applicant pool for the mechatronics pathway during its critical launch phase. The decline was not unique to HCCC but reflected a regional pattern in the Mid-South, where rural communities faced compounded economic pressures. A more specific operational challenge arose within the Department of Mechatronics and Industrial Automation. An unexpected instructor vacancy occurred during the third year of the project (2023-2024). This position was critical for delivering core sequence courses required for program completion. The delay in filling this vacancy resulted in a pause in course offerings for approximately one academic year. For students already enrolled, this created bottlenecks in their progression through the curriculum. Many were forced to defer their enrollment or reduce their course loads, extending the time to completion. For new applicants, the lack of available sections discouraged enrollment, as the program’s continuity appeared uncertain. This operational hiccup effectively compressed the window for student accumulation, contributing directly to the shortfall in final completers. Despite the missed target on completions, the project succeeded in building substantial infrastructure and partnerships that will support future workforce development efforts. 2. Clarify/verify "other directly impacting awards" status
3. Obtain current Northgate letter referencing SATP
